anomalyExplanations.unrecorded-fulfillment-revenue: Roost & Bean pays postage on shipped orders all quarter, yet shipping income never once appears in the books — even though a third of the order memos say the customer paid for shipping. That collected money is arriving bundled into product deposits and going unbooked, quietly understating revenue on every shipped order. Worth a look: book collected shipping as its own line so the books match what customers actually paid.
anomalyExplanations.price-variance: The same wholesale item sold to three different cafes at three materially different prices across the quarter. That can be intentional — volume discounts, long-standing relationships — but if it isn't, it's margin quietly leaking on every discounted invoice. Worth a look: set a written wholesale price list, and note any agreed discount on the invoice memo so the difference is documented.
anomalyExplanations.commingling: A game controller and a beach stay were paid from the business account. Mixing personal and business spending is the most common bookkeeping problem for small operators — it muddies real margins and creates tax-time pain. Worth a look: move personal spending to a personal account, or record it as an owner draw the moment it happens, which is where these are currently booked.
anomalyExplanations.duplicate-charge: Adobe charged the identical subscription amount twice on the same day. Sometimes that's legitimate — two seats, two products — but it's often a billing error or a double-submitted payment. Worth a look: check the Adobe invoice history, and dispute the second charge if it doesn't match.
anomalyExplanations.vendor-aging: A green-coffee supplier invoice was settled well past the due date printed on its memo. Late payments strain the supplier relationships a small roaster depends on, and some vendors add late fees. Worth a look: a reminder a few days before each due date keeps this from recurring — the operations page can draft one.
anomalyExplanations.round-number-cash: An identical round cash deposit lands once a month, every month. That may be perfectly normal for the farmers-market stall — the point is documentation. Worth a look: keep a simple daily cash log with the register total and deposit amount, so every deposit traces to recorded sales.
